Methods and statistics

How psychology is researched: designs, samples, uncertainty, correlation and causation, replication.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Psychology is a science because it tests its ideas against data. To do so it uses observation, surveys, experiments and studies over time, and statistics to know whether a result is reliable or could be due to chance. Knowing these methods helps us read "a study shows that..." headlines with a critical eye.

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

Kinds of study

  • Descriptive: observations, surveys and case studies, which describe how things are.
  • Correlational: measure whether two variables go together, for example hours of sleep and mood.
  • Experimental: the researcher changes one variable and assigns people to groups at random. It is the best way to know whether one thing causes another.
  • Longitudinal: follow the same people for years.

Correlation is not causation

Two things going together does not mean one causes the other. It may be the other way round, or a third variable may explain both. In summer, ice-cream sales and drownings rise together, and the culprit is the heat.

Samples

A study with few people, or with very similar people, may produce results that do not generalise. Much research has been done with university students in Western countries.

Uncertainty

No study gives absolute certainty. Confidence intervals show the range of values compatible with the data, and the effect size shows how much a difference matters, not just whether it exists. A result becomes solid when it is replicated in independent studies.

Effect size

Knowing that a treatment "works" is not enough: we need to know how much. Effect size expresses this. By convention a Cohen's d of 0.2 is considered small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large, although what matters is what it means in practice. A small effect can be very relevant if it affects millions of people or is cheap to deliver.

Research ethics

After abuses such as the Tuskegee syphilis study and some psychological experiments, rules were established: informed consent, the right to withdraw, confidentiality and review by ethics committees. When a study needs to deceive participants, they must be told afterwards what happened.

Qualitative and quantitative

Quantitative methods measure and count; qualitative ones, such as in-depth interviews or focus groups, explore how people experience and make sense of something. They are not rivals: the latter help generate questions and the former help test them.

Placebo and double-blinding

To know whether a treatment works it is not enough to see whether people improve: many would improve anyway with time, with the attention received or because of their expectations. That is why it is compared with a control group, often given a placebo, and each person is assigned at random. In a double-blind trial, neither participants nor assessors know who gets what, so that expectations do not influence the results. In psychotherapy it is hard to blind patients, so trials must be interpreted with more caution.

Regression to the mean

People tend to come to the clinic when they are at their worst. As many problems fluctuate, they are likely to be somewhat better next time, whatever is done. This phenomenon, described by Francis Galton, is called regression to the mean: extreme values tend to be followed by values closer to the average. It explains why so many remedies seem to work and why a control group is needed to know whether something really helps.

What a p-value means (and does not)

The p-value indicates how often data at least as extreme would be obtained if there were in fact no effect. It does not give the probability that the hypothesis is true, nor how important the effect is. In 2016 the American Statistical Association published a statement warning against its misuse and reminding that "p < 0.05" should not be the sole basis for conclusions.

Level 3 · Going further, with references

In the nineteenth century Francis Galton introduced the ideas of correlation and regression to the mean; Karl Pearson formalised the correlation coefficient. In the 1920s and 1930s Ronald Fisher developed experimental design with random assignment and analysis of variance. Significance testing with the famous p < 0.05 threshold became a ritual that many statisticians have criticised.

In 2011 a paper by Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn showed that, with small flexible decisions in analysis, it was possible to get "significant" results for almost anything (p-hacking). Together with replication failures, this drove reforms: pre-registration of hypotheses and analyses before collecting data, registered reports accepted by journals before results are known, sharing data and materials, and studies with much larger samples.

Meta-analyses, which combine the results of many studies, are the basis of the strongest conclusions, though they can be distorted by publication bias, since negative results are published less often. Bayesian statistics offers an alternative that quantifies how much the data support one hypothesis over another.

Open debates: how to balance rigour with research in real-world settings; what thresholds of evidence to require; and how to communicate uncertainty to the public without breeding distrust.

Causal inference without experiments

Random assignment is not always possible: we cannot make some people smoke and others not. For these cases there are designs such as natural experiments (exploiting changes that happen by chance, such as a law coming into force in one region but not another), discordant twin studies and Mendelian randomisation, which uses genetic variants as a kind of natural lottery.

Open science

Sharing data, analysis code and materials lets others check results. Registered reports, in which a journal accepts the article before the results are known, reduce publication bias. In them, the proportion of confirmed hypotheses is much lower than in traditional articles, which suggests how much the old system inflated results.

Systematic reviews and meta-analysis

A single study is rarely enough. A systematic review searches for all studies on a question using an explicit, reproducible method, and a meta-analysis combines their results to obtain a more precise estimate. Gene Glass coined the term in 1976 precisely to summarise studies on the effectiveness of psychotherapy. The Cochrane Collaboration, founded in 1993, made these reviews the basis of evidence-based medicine.

The studies that go unpublished

If studies with positive results are published more often than negative ones, the literature exaggerates how well treatments work. In 2008, antidepressant trials registered with the US Food and Drug Administration were compared with those published: almost all positive ones were published, while many negative ones were not, or were presented as positive. The apparent effect in the literature was about a third larger than the real one. Registering trials before they begin helps prevent this.
